svg.title: Three curves, three equivalence points
svg.desc: Three titration curves drawn on the same axes, pH against millilitres of titrant added, each starting from fifty millilitres of 0.10 molar analyte titrated with 0.10 molar titrant, so every equivalence point falls at fifty millilitres. The first curve is 0.10 molar hydrochloric acid titrated with sodium hydroxide: it begins at pH 1, creeps upward with no flat region at all, jumps almost vertically at fifty millilitres through an equivalence point at exactly pH 7, and levels off above pH 12. The second is 0.10 molar acetic acid titrated with sodium hydroxide: it begins near pH 2.9, far higher than the strong acid because the acid is only partly dissociated, flattens into a long buffering region whose midpoint at twenty-five millilitres sits at pH 4.76, the pKa, then rises through an equivalence point at about pH 8.7, which is above seven because everything in the flask is now acetate, a weak base. The third is 0.10 molar ammonia titrated with hydrochloric acid, which runs downward: it begins near pH 11.1, flattens through a buffering region whose midpoint at twenty-five millilitres sits at pH 9.25, the pKa of ammonium, then falls through an equivalence point near pH 5.3, which is below seven because everything in the flask is now ammonium, a weak acid. Markers show the half-equivalence point of each weak curve, where the pH equals the pKa and the curve is flattest, and the equivalence point of each. Beyond the equivalence point the two base-titrated curves converge, since both are then simply solutions of excess sodium hydroxide. A panel beside the plot lists what the shape tells you: the starting pH separates a strong acid near pH one from a weak acid several units higher; a flat pre-equivalence stretch means a weak acid or weak base, and its midpoint reads off the pKa directly; the equivalence pH is seven for strong against strong, above seven for a weak acid against a strong base, and below seven for a weak base against a strong acid; and the jump is taller and sharper for the strong acid and for more concentrated solutions. A footer warns that the slow early rise of a strong acid curve is not buffering: there is no conjugate pair present, and the rise is gentle only because pH is logarithmic, so removing a small fraction of a large hydrogen ion concentration barely moves the logarithm.
svg.text: The equivalence point is where the moles match — not where the pH is 7. What sits in the flask at that moment decides the pH.

The slow start of the strong-acid curve is not buffering
There is no conjugate pair in the flask — nothing to absorb added base. The rise is gentle only because pH is logarithmic:
neutralising a small fraction of a large [H⁺] barely shifts the log. Call it a buffer and you will misread what the flat
stretch of a weak-acid curve actually means.
